paragraphs: This paper investigates whether machine learning can turn brain signals measured by magnetoencephalography, or MEG, into commands for an interactive computer interface. The researchers train classifiers on signals recorded while people imagine movements. The central question is whether the learned distinction can support actual online interaction, rather than only classify previously collected recordings.

The study applies RCE and regularized support vector machines to experimental data from ten healthy participants. Four participants subsequently used a trained classifier to write a short name. This provides a concrete demonstration that the recorded signals and learned classifiers could work together in an operating interface for some participants.

The authors also position MEG as a way to assess whether an electroencephalography interface might succeed, since training with the latter may be slower because of lower signal quality. Their analysis suggests that the chosen imagery task is suboptimal for extending the interface to multiple classes. They describe the system as a proof of concept and, to their knowledge, the first working online MEG interface.
icml-2005-a-brain-computer-interface-wit.tldr: A MEG-based brain interface let four of ten participants write a short name using learned classifiers of imagined movements.

paragraphs: A support vector machine represents its solution using a collection of support vectors. This paper proposes simplifying that representation by reducing how many vectors it needs. The aim is to retain the machine’s ability to generalize while replacing a more elaborate solution with a smaller one.

The reduction proceeds iteratively. At each step, the method selects two nearest support vectors from the same class and replaces them with a newly constructed vector. The construction uses an analysis of the relationship between vectors in the original input space and their representations in feature space. This makes the replacement a specific mathematical operation rather than simply discarding one member of the pair.

The resulting construction requires finding the unique maximum of a function of one variable within the interval from zero to one. The authors contrast this with earlier reduced-set methods that minimize functions of many variables with local minima. Experiments on real datasets show that the method reduces support-vector counts while preserving generalization performance in the evaluated cases.
icml-2005-an-efficient-method-for-simpli.tldr: Iteratively merging nearby support vectors from the same class simplifies SVMs while preserving generalization in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Markov decision processes provide a framework for planning, but realistic problems can contain too many states to examine exhaustively. This paper focuses on a narrower requirement: finding a partial policy that gets an agent from a fixed starting state to a goal. For that task, computation can concentrate on relevant states rather than cover every possible situation.

The proposed algorithm, Bounded RTDP, maintains both upper and lower bounds on the optimal value function. These bounds give the planner information about how good the optimal outcome could be, supporting performance guarantees for the partial policy it produces. The algorithm can obtain such guarantees while visiting only part of the state space, including on problems where other algorithms would visit all of it.

A further contribution is an efficient technique for finding suitable upper bounds, which substantially helps Bounded RTDP’s performance. The authors also identify this technique as useful for initializing other planning algorithms. The contribution therefore combines focused planning with bounds that make the quality of the resulting partial policy assessable.
icml-2005-bounded-real-time-dynamic-prog.tldr: Bounded RTDP uses upper and lower value bounds to produce partial planning policies with performance guarantees while exploring only relevant portions of a state space.

paragraphs: Different clustering methods can divide the same objects into different groups, creating a need for criteria that compare those divisions. This paper examines what such criteria mean mathematically. It treats clusterings as elements of a lattice of partitions and studies how distances between clusterings relate to that structure.

From this perspective, the authors give axiomatic characterizations of several comparison criteria, including variation of information and the unadjusted Rand index. An axiomatic characterization explains a criterion through the properties it satisfies. This provides a way to understand and compare measures beyond simply looking at their numerical outputs on particular examples.

The paper then tests other partition distances against these axioms and proves an impossibility result. Within its notion of a sensible comparison criterion, no measure can simultaneously align with the partition lattice, satisfy convex additivity, and remain bounded. The finding identifies a tradeoff among these three requirements: a comparison measure cannot satisfy the entire combination, so choosing among measures also involves choosing which properties to retain.
icml-2005-comparing-clusterings-an-axiom.tldr: An axiomatic analysis of clustering comparisons proves that lattice alignment, convex additivity, and boundedness cannot all hold together.

paragraphs: When predicting one discrete variable from another, a common approach assigns a separate outcome distribution to every possible input state. This is flexible, but it can sacrifice statistical power when many states could share a simpler description. The paper studies a model that groups input states into disjoint sets and assigns one Dirichlet-multinomial model to each group.

The grouping itself is unknown. Instead of choosing a single partition and treating it as settled, the authors integrate over possible partitions when addressing broader tasks such as variable selection or classification. This keeps uncertainty about the grouping within the calculation used for the final task.

The main contribution is computational: two exact algorithms, based on different approaches, perform this integration. The authors derive complexity bounds that depend on detailed problem characteristics, including dataset size and the number of input states. Synthetic-data experiments demonstrate that the algorithms can be applied in practice. Together, these results explain how to compute with the partition model and how its computational demands depend on the problem.
icml-2005-computational-aspects-of-bayes.tldr: Two exact algorithms integrate over uncertain groupings of discrete input states in Bayesian partition models.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning usually expresses success through a single numerical reward. Many decisions instead involve several objectives, and the importance assigned to each objective can change over time. This paper studies learning under those changing preferences, representing the current importance of the objectives with numerical weights.

The proposed method stores a finite collection of policies. Given a weight vector, it selects an appropriate policy from that collection and can improve upon it. The motivation is that infinitely many possible preference settings may still be covered well by a small number of optimal policies. A separate stored policy for every possible weight vector may therefore be unnecessary.

The authors investigate this idea empirically in a version of the Buridan’s ass problem and in network routing. These examples support the possibility that a compact policy collection can serve a broad range of preferences. The result concerns adapting behavior as priorities change, with the empirical evidence supporting small collections in the studied domains rather than establishing that every multi-objective problem has such a compact representation.
icml-2005-dynamic-preferences-in-multi-c.tldr: A finite collection of policies can support changing objective weights by providing a policy to select and improve for each preference setting.

paragraphs: Regression involves estimating how an output changes with its inputs, but observations can also differ in how noisy they are. This paper presents an algorithm that estimates both the mean response and the variance in a nonparametric regression problem. Its central feature is estimating variance locally, allowing the estimated noise level to vary across the input space.

Local variance estimation matters because a prediction of the average response does not describe how widely observations fluctuate around that response. By estimating both quantities together, the method adapts to local noise. The authors identify this capability as a difference from standard Gaussian process regression and support vector machines.

The estimation problem is formulated using maximum a posteriori estimation within exponential families. This combines the estimation of mean and variance in a single mathematical framework. The authors obtain a convex optimization problem, contrasting their formulation with previous work, and state that it can be solved with Newton’s method. The contribution thus concerns both what the model estimates and how the joint estimation problem can be computed.
icml-2005-heteroscedastic-gaussian-proce.tldr: The paper jointly estimates regression means and locally varying noise through a convex optimization formulation.

paragraphs: This paper addresses steering a remote-control car at high speed through unstructured outdoor environments. Its approach connects two learned components: a vision system that estimates obstacle depth from a single image and a control policy that uses the vision system’s output to choose a steering direction.

The vision component is trained through supervised learning. Training examples can be real camera images labeled with measured distances to the nearest obstacles, or synthetic images generated with graphics. The resulting algorithm learns visual cues that estimate the relative depths of obstacles in a scene. This supplies depth information from individual monocular images for the steering component.

The control policy is learned using reinforcement learning or policy search inside a simulator that renders synthetic scenes. It learns how to turn the vision system’s output into steering decisions. The authors evaluate predictive ability on held-out data and report actual autonomous driving experiments. These evaluations connect the depth-estimation component with the broader driving task, while the overall method shows how supervised perception and simulated policy learning can be combined.
icml-2005-high-speed-obstacle-avoidance-.tldr: A car learns to steer around obstacles by combining depth estimates from single images with a control policy trained in simulation.

paragraphs: In a first-order probabilistic model, a variable can have many parent variables once the model is expanded into a concrete network. The number of parents can also vary. This makes it useful to describe influences compactly, without specifying a separate full conditional distribution for every possible collection of parents.

One approach describes the target’s probability conditioned on each individual parent, or on small parent groups, and then combines those distributions using a rule such as NoisyOR. This separates the description of individual influences from the mechanism that combines them. The paper develops algorithms for learning within this representation.

The authors derive and implement learning methods based on gradient descent and expectation maximization. They evaluate the methods using synthetic data and a real-world task. The reported results show that the algorithms can learn parameters for both the parent-to-target distributions and the combining rules. This matters because the overall model depends on both pieces: how each parent influences the target and how those influences are brought together.
icml-2005-learning-first-order-probabili.tldr: Gradient-based and expectation-maximization algorithms learn both individual influences and the rules that combine them in first-order probabilistic models.

paragraphs: Markov logic networks combine logical clauses with numerical weights, using the clauses as templates for features in a probabilistic network. This paper addresses how to learn which clauses should be included from relational databases. It combines ideas from inductive logic programming and feature induction in Markov networks.

The algorithm searches through possible clauses using either beam search or a search that considers shorter clauses first. A weighted pseudo-likelihood measure guides its choice among candidate structures. Evaluating those structures requires finding their optimal weights, and the authors show how to perform this step efficiently. Structure selection and weight estimation are therefore connected within the learning procedure.

The method can build a network from scratch or refine an existing knowledge base. In two real-world domains, the authors report better performance than using off-the-shelf inductive logic programming systems to select the network structure. They also report improvements over purely logical, purely probabilistic, and purely knowledge-based approaches. These findings support jointly learning logical structure and probabilistic weights in the evaluated settings.
icml-2005-learning-the-structure-of-mark.tldr: A clause-search algorithm learns Markov logic network structure and weights, outperforming several alternative approaches in two real-world domains.

paragraphs: Supervised learning commonly assumes that training and test examples come from the same distribution. This paper relaxes that requirement for logistic regression. It considers a fully labeled auxiliary dataset and a partially labeled primary dataset drawn from a different distribution, with the goal of filling in the primary dataset’s missing labels.

The proposed method, Migratory-Logit or M-Logit, introduces an auxiliary variable for each example in the auxiliary dataset. These variables represent how the auxiliary examples mismatch the primary data. Under an appropriate constraint, the method estimates them along with the classifier. The distribution mismatch is therefore represented within training instead of treating both sources as interchangeable.

The paper also presents an active learning approach for choosing which primary examples to label. This addresses how to obtain supervision from the distribution where predictions are needed, alongside using the already labeled auxiliary source. Demonstrations on simulated and real datasets are reported as successful. The contribution is a logistic-regression method for combining these two sources while explicitly accounting for their mismatch.
icml-2005-logistic-regression-with-an-au.tldr: M-Logit learns from a labeled auxiliary source while estimating its mismatch with the partially labeled dataset it aims to complete.

paragraphs: Words often appear in bursts within a document: once a word occurs, further occurrences become more likely. The paper argues that the multinomial distributions commonly used for text do not capture this behavior well. It proposes the Dirichlet compound multinomial, or DCM, as an alternative document model.

The DCM has one additional degree of freedom that enables it to represent burstiness. This gives the model a way to account for repetition as part of its probability distribution. The change directly addresses a stated property of text, making the modeling choice depend on how word occurrences behave within documents.

Experiments show substantially better text modeling than the multinomial when measured by perplexity. On three standard document collections, the DCM also improves classification over the multinomial model. Its performance is comparable to a multinomial model augmented with several heuristic modifications. Together, these findings show benefits both for assigning probabilities to text and for classifying documents, with the additional modeling flexibility providing an alternative to those heuristic adjustments.
icml-2005-modeling-word-burstiness-using.tldr: A Dirichlet compound multinomial captures repeated-word bursts and improves text modeling and document classification in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Naive Bayes models are commonly used for classification and clustering. This paper asks whether they are also useful for broader probability estimation: computing joint probabilities, conditional probabilities, and marginal probabilities. That shifts attention from predicting a class label to answering different probabilistic questions with a learned model.

The authors learn naive Bayes models using expectation maximization and compare them with Bayesian networks that represent context-specific independence. Across a wide range of benchmark datasets, the naive Bayes models achieve comparable accuracy and training time. This establishes an empirical basis for considering their simpler model structure for these broader tasks.

The largest reported difference concerns inference, the computation of probabilities after learning. Naive Bayes inference is orders of magnitude faster than the compared Bayesian network inference using Gibbs sampling and belief propagation. The authors therefore present naive Bayes as an attractive alternative for large or real-time domains. The practical significance lies in the combination observed in their evaluation: comparable probability-estimation accuracy and learning time, together with substantially faster inference.
icml-2005-naive-bayes-models-for-probabi.tldr: Naive Bayes models learned with EM deliver comparable probability-estimation accuracy and much faster inference than the evaluated Bayesian network methods.

paragraphs: This paper extends PAC-Bayes theory to classifiers represented through sample compression. Each classifier is specified by two independent information sources: a small subset of the training examples and a message containing the extra information needed to reconstruct the classifier. The theoretical problem is to bound risk for classifiers described in this way.

The authors construct a prior over a set of objects that does not depend on the observed data. Each object produces a classifier only once the training data is supplied. This distinction between a data-independent object and the classifier it later defines provides the basis for the new bound in the sample-compression setting.

The resulting theorem applies to a Gibbs classifier defined through a posterior distribution over compressed classifiers. It shows that this randomized classifier can receive a smaller risk bound than any individual deterministic compressed classifier under consideration. The statement concerns a possible improvement in the bound, rather than a guarantee of lower actual error in every case. It gives a theoretical reason to consider distributions over compressed classifiers alongside single compressed solutions.
icml-2005-pac-bayes-risk-bounds-for-samp.tldr: A PAC-Bayes extension shows that a Gibbs distribution over sample-compressed classifiers can have a tighter risk bound than individual deterministic classifiers.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether the numbers produced by learning algorithms correspond well to posterior probabilities. The focus is probability calibration: whether predicted probabilities faithfully express uncertainty. The authors compare the distortions associated with different learning methods and investigate ways to correct them.

They find that maximum-margin methods such as boosted trees and boosted stumps move probability mass away from zero and one, producing a characteristic sigmoid-shaped distortion. Naive Bayes models with unrealistic independence assumptions show the opposite tendency, pushing probabilities toward those extremes. Neural networks and bagged trees are reported to avoid these biases and produce well-calibrated probabilities.

The authors study Platt scaling and isotonic regression as corrections for biased probability predictions. They examine which types of distortion suit each method and how much data is needed for calibration to be effective. In their empirical results, calibrated boosted trees, random forests, and support vector machines produce the best probabilities. The findings make calibration part of evaluating a learning method, since the quality of its probability estimates can change after correction.
icml-2005-predicting-good-probabilities-.tldr: Different learners distort probabilities differently, and calibration gives boosted trees, random forests, and SVMs the best probability estimates in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Recognizing protein folds helps connect amino-acid sequences with three-dimensional structure. This paper focuses on folds containing interacting structural repeats. Existing approaches can struggle with long-range interactions between structural units and with proteins whose sequences share less than 25 percent identity, making these folds difficult to recognize from sequence alone.

The authors propose a chain graph model built from a causally connected series of segmentation conditional random fields. These fields represent long-range interactions within recurring structural units. A Bayesian network backbone decomposes interactions between repeats into locally computable modules, combining repeat-specific fields with a model of sequence motifs.

The model is applied to predicting beta-helices and leucine-rich repeats. The authors report significant improvements over existing methods in predictive accuracy, computational efficiency, or both. The contribution connects two needs: representing dependencies that are important for repeated protein structures and organizing those dependencies into computations that can be handled locally. The reported findings support this combination for the two types of repeated structures evaluated.
icml-2005-predicting-protein-folds-with-.tldr: A chain graph models interactions within and between protein repeats, improving accuracy and/or computational efficiency for two evaluated fold types.

paragraphs: Choosing a classification algorithm can involve estimating how competing methods will perform before carrying out extensive experiments. This paper studies predictions of relative performance using results from small data samples. It discusses weaknesses in earlier approaches and proposes a variant based on metalearning, using information from previously completed learning experiments.

The new method first runs experiments on a few samples. It uses the resulting observations to identify the nearest learning curve among curves whose sampling procedures have already been completed. That matched curve then supplies information for predicting the relative performance of the classification algorithms.

The approach matters because a limited set of observations is connected to a more complete record of how learning progressed elsewhere. It uses that connection to make a comparative prediction without requiring the full sampling procedure for the new case. The experimental evaluation finds that the method competes well with previous approaches and offers a practical solution. The stated result supports its usefulness for comparative algorithm assessment, without claiming that every predicted ranking will be correct.
icml-2005-predicting-relative-performanc.tldr: Matching a few sample-based results to previously completed learning curves helps predict which classification algorithms will perform better.

paragraphs: This paper proposes learning reusable building blocks for value functions from the structure of a state space. These building blocks, called proto-value functions, are independent of a particular reward task. The framework learns them by analyzing the topology of the state space rather than deriving them from rewards.

Mathematically, proto-value functions are Fourier eigenfunctions of the Laplace-Beltrami diffusion operator on the state-space manifold. They form an orthonormal basis whose smoothness follows the geometry of that space. The paper uses this structure both to decompose large state spaces and to provide basis functions for approximating value functions.

The theoretical framework brings together spectral graph theory, harmonic analysis, and Riemannian geometry. Its reinforcement-learning consequence is a family of algorithms called representation policy iteration, which connects learning a representation with learning behavior. The key contribution is to make the state space itself a source of representation: its topology supplies task-independent components that can be used when constructing value functions for particular rewards. This places representation learning inside the process of learning a policy.
icml-2005-proto-value-functions-developm.tldr: Proto-value functions learn task-independent value-function building blocks from state-space geometry, linking representation learning with policy learning.

paragraphs: This paper establishes a quantitative relationship between reinforcement learning and binary classification. It connects a policy’s expected total reward to the predictive performance of classifiers on constructed subproblems. This makes classification performance a mathematically grounded way to reason about the quality of the resulting policy.

The connection does not require assumptions of independence, short mixing times, fully observable states, or even hidden states. The resulting statement also does not depend on the number of states or actions. Its critical dependencies are instead the size of rewards and the prediction performance achieved on the constructed classification problems.

The paper also discusses how to obtain good classifiers for those subproblems, including possible ways to generate training examples for a classification learner. This practical component matters because the theoretical connection depends directly on prediction quality. The contribution therefore combines a broad performance relationship with guidance about the data needed to use it. It identifies reward scale and classifier performance as central quantities without requiring the listed assumptions about the environment.
icml-2005-relating-reinforcement-learnin.tldr: A theorem links policy reward to binary classification performance without dependence on the number of states or actions.

paragraphs: An ROC curve summarizes classifier performance, but an estimated curve is uncertain. This paper evaluates confidence bands intended to contain the true curve at a specified confidence level. The authors introduce three methods from medical research and examine whether their bands achieve reasonable containment.

They begin with synthetic data whose class-conditional scores follow normal distributions, making the true ROC curve known. Only the nonparametric fixed-width bands achieve reasonable containment without modification. The authors then consider a different target: bounding a model’s performance on future data. They introduce a correction for the additional uncertainty, and the resulting wider fixed-width bands continue to show reasonable containment.

The study also evaluates the bands on ten relatively large benchmark datasets. The authors recommend fixed-width bands, emphasizing their nonparametric nature. In their machine-learning evaluations, score distributions are clearly nonnormal and can differ substantially between learning methods even on the same dataset. The recommendation therefore reflects both observed containment and suitability for varying score distributions, while the correction distinguishes uncertainty about the underlying curve from uncertainty about future performance.
icml-2005-roc-confidence-bands-an-empiri.tldr: An empirical comparison favors nonparametric fixed-width ROC confidence bands, with a widening correction when bounding future-data performance.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised clustering uses limited supervision, often expressed as constraints on pairs of objects, to guide grouping. Such constraints fit graph data naturally, yet many methods are designed for vectors. This paper develops a kernel formulation that connects clustering in these two representations.

The authors show that a Hidden Markov Random Field clustering objective becomes a special case of weighted kernel k-means when squared Euclidean distance and a particular class of constraint penalties are used. A theoretical connection between kernel k-means and graph clustering then allows the formulation to handle either vectors or graphs. For vector data, kernels also permit cluster boundaries that are nonlinear in the original input space.

The formulation additionally includes earlier spectral-learning work as a special case. These connections show how several approaches can be understood within a shared objective, with the stated conditions governing the equivalence. Empirical results show that the proposed algorithm can outperform contemporary semi-supervised methods on both vector and graph datasets. The contribution combines this evaluated performance with a mathematical bridge between previously separate clustering approaches.
icml-2005-semi-supervised-graph-clusteri.tldr: A weighted kernel k-means formulation connects constrained vector and graph clustering and achieves strong empirical results on both.

paragraphs: This paper studies binary classification with support vector machines while directly penalizing the number of support vectors in the solution. It uses this count, described as an L0 regularization term, in place of the more usual L1 or L2 terms. The objective therefore explicitly favors solutions represented by fewer support vectors.

To solve the resulting optimization problem, the authors apply the cross entropy method to search over possible support-vector sets. The algorithm works through a sequence of efficient linear programs. This supplies a computational approach for selecting the set itself, bringing the desired reduction in representation size into the optimization process.

The reported experiments produce generalization errors similar to those of support vector machines while using considerably fewer support vectors. The significance is the observed balance between a smaller solution and retained predictive performance on new examples. The paper thus demonstrates that directly regularizing the support-vector count can yield compact classifiers in the evaluated cases, with the cross entropy search and linear programs providing the mechanism for obtaining them.
icml-2005-the-cross-entropy-method-for-c.tldr: Cross entropy search directly penalizes support-vector counts, producing smaller classifiers with similar generalization error in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Biological claims can be supported by several different kinds of evidence, and databases often collect these claims for later analysis. Automatically making preliminary inclusion decisions can be useful when the decisions are sufficiently accurate. This paper addresses how to weigh evidence sources whose strength may differ.

The proposed algorithm learns a scoring function by examining how much support each evidence source receives from other sources. Cross-source support therefore helps determine the contribution of different evidence types to the overall score. A probabilistic formulation, building on earlier theoretical work, guides the details of the method.

The authors evaluate the method on protein-protein interaction prediction in yeast and on synthetic data. These applications examine evidence integration both in a biological task and in constructed data. The contribution is a method for learning how to combine heterogeneous evidence without making source weights solely a matter of manual choice. Its role in the database setting is to support preliminary selection of propositions by turning patterns of support across sources into a learned scoring function.
icml-2005-unsupervised-evidence-integrat.tldr: An unsupervised scoring method weights evidence sources according to how strongly other sources support them.

paragraphs: Online learning becomes harder when the relationship being learned changes over time. This paper introduces AddExp, an additive expert ensemble method designed to use an online learner under such concept drift. It also changes the reference point used to assess performance over a subsequence of the training data.

Earlier expert-prediction analyses compare worst-case performance with the best expert on a subsequence, but those experts may be difficult to implement. The authors instead bound performance relative to what an actual online learner achieves on that same subsequence. This makes the comparison depend on an operational learning procedure and its observed performance over the relevant segment.

Using techniques adapted from expert-prediction analysis, the paper proves mistake and loss bounds for discrete and continuous versions of AddExp. It also presents pruning methods and empirical results on datasets with concept drift. The contribution combines a general way to use online learners for changing targets with theoretical guarantees framed around their actual subsequence performance, alongside empirical investigation of the ensemble approach.
icml-2005-using-additive-expert-ensemble.tldr: AddExp adapts online learners to concept drift with mistake and loss bounds relative to a learner’s actual performance on a subsequence.

paragraphs: This paper introduces weighted decomposition kernels for comparing discrete structured objects. The basic approach divides each object into substructures and builds a similarity measure from matches between those parts. Each substructure has a selector that determines whether it can be matched with a substructure from another object.

A match occurs when the selectors satisfy an equality condition. The importance of that match is then determined by a probability kernel applied to local distributions fitted to the substructures. The method therefore separates eligibility for matching from the weight assigned to the match, combining structural decomposition with information from local probability distributions.

Under reasonable assumptions, the authors show that these kernels can be computed efficiently and can avoid a combinatorial explosion in the feature space. Experiments on a set of bioinformatics problems find the proposed kernel highly competitive with more complex contemporary methods. The contribution is a family of structured-data similarities that combines selective matching and probability-based weighting, with conditional computational advantages and empirical evidence of competitive performance.
icml-2005-weighted-decomposition-kernels.tldr: Weighted decomposition kernels compare selected substructures using local probability distributions and show competitive results on bioinformatics problems.
